A Romanian story, told from Europe’s border

Europe,
seen from the edge

At the centre, Europe can look permanent. On its borders, it has always been a choice.

Georgia, 2024Ukraine, 2013
Begin the story ↓
PrologueAt Europe’s unfinished edge

In Tbilisi, a blue flag with twelve stars rises above the smoke. In Kyiv, it rises beside the blue and yellow.

These are not people asking to become someone else. They are claiming the right to choose what power may do to them, how their states will be governed, and which future their children will inherit.

Ukraine’s path to the European Union now runs through war. Georgia’s has been thrown into crisis. Seen from Paris or Berlin, accession can sound like procedure. Seen from a border, Europe is a promise that a smaller country will not be left alone with a larger empire.

Romania knows this promise by its absence.

IA country before the country

The frontier came first.

In the eighteenth century, there was no Romanian state. There were principalities, provinces, courts, villages and churches, held inside the ambitions of larger powers.

The Ottoman Empire held suzerainty over Moldavia and Wallachia. The Habsburg world governed Transylvania and, later, Bukovina. From the east came a Russian Empire moving toward the Black Sea, the Danube and the Balkans.

Geography was not destiny. But it set the table at which other states expected to divide the meal.

1812

Russia annexed the eastern half of Moldavia—the land that would be called Bessarabia—through a treaty with the Ottoman Empire. Moldavia was not at the table.

IIThe nation begins as a sentence

Before Romania had borders, it found a direction.

It found it in language: a Romance tongue surviving far from the other Romance nations, carrying the memory of Latin through a predominantly Slavic and imperial world.

Ромынromân

Scholars of the Transylvanian School argued for Roman origins. The Latin alphabet gradually replaced Cyrillic. French and Italian supplied a vocabulary for public life, science, law and modern feeling.

This was not a recovery of some untouched past. It was an act of construction: a people choosing the family of ideas in which it wished to speak.

Paris, 1848

Ideas cross borders before armies do.

Young Moldavians and Wallachians encountered the French Revolution’s descendants: citizenship, constitutional rule, national self-determination and the belief that history could be made—not only endured.

They returned with books, friendships, ambitions and a tricolour. Europe entered Romanian life through translation, fashion, argument, architecture and law. France became less a foreign country than a vocabulary for the possible.

IIIThe borrowed prince

Bucharest, 1866

A young country chose a German dynasty to become more securely itself.

Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen arrived from the German world to lead a fragile union. His foreign name was part of the point: dynastic legitimacy, diplomatic weight and distance from the rivalries of local elites.

Under Carol I, Romania gained independence, became a kingdom, laid railways and built institutions intended to outlast a generation. The experiment joined Romanian national ambition to a European architecture of law, monarchy and statecraft.

But on the edge of Europe, every alliance carried a contradiction.

Romania fought beside Russia against the Ottoman Empire in 1877–78. It emerged independent—and still had to surrender southern Bessarabia to its ally, receiving Northern Dobruja in exchange.

In 1883, fear of Russian pressure helped drive Romania into a secret defensive alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary. Yet Austria-Hungary ruled millions of Romanians in Transylvania. There was no pure choice, only the search for room to remain sovereign.

IVThe map breaks

The state grew. The guarantees failed.

The First World War and the settlements of 1918 brought most Romanian-speaking lands into one state. The achievement was vast; so were the new obligations to minorities and democracy.

The interwar promise fractured under economic crisis, authoritarianism and fascism. Romania’s fear of empire did not prevent crimes committed in Romania’s own name: the persecution and murder of Jews and Roma, including in Romanian-administered Transnistria, belong inside this history.

June 1940

The Soviet Union delivered an ultimatum. Romanian forces were ordered out of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina within four days.

A border that had seemed fixed vanished in the time between one train timetable and the next.

After annexation

Empire does not end when the frontier moves.

01

Borders are redrawn and regions divided.

02

Institutions and public language are remade.

03

Elites are removed; memory is disciplined.

04

People are settled, classified, deported.

35,796

people were deported from the Moldavian SSR in the mass operation of July 1949. Nearly twelve thousand were children.

After 1944, Romania itself entered the Soviet sphere. Political opponents disappeared into prisons. Property was nationalised, villages collectivised, history rewritten. The country remained on the map while much of its sovereignty moved elsewhere.

VThe long return

Europe was not a new destination.

After 1989, Romania did not simply travel west. It returned to a conversation its writers, revolutionaries and state-builders had entered two centuries before.

NATO membership in 2004 and European Union membership in 2007 did not end history. They answered an old Romanian question with new institutions: how can a state at the border remain free without remaining alone?

✦✦✦✦✦
together

This is why Ukraine is not remote from Romania’s peace. The issue is larger than sympathy and nearer than charity: whether a border may again be changed by force, and whether a nation may choose its own alliances without punishment from an empire.

Georgia and Ukraine stand today where European ideals are not ceremonial. They are contested. Their struggle reminds the rest of the continent that Europe survives only when its principles reach its edges.

A perspective from the border

From the centre,
Europe can look permanent.

From its edges, it never has.

European unity is not the end of national cultures. It is what allows them to meet without conquest—and to remain themselves.

Romania’s history is not only a story about joining Europe. It is a story Europe may need in order to remember itself.
